Stateful Reasoning via Insight Replay

Bin Lei Affiliation: University of Minnesota    Caiwen Ding Affiliation: University of Minnesota    Jiachen Yang Affiliation: Simular AI    Ang Li Affiliation: Simular AI    Xin Eric Wang Corresponding author: Bin Lei (lei00126@umn.edu), Xin Eric Wang (eric@simular.ai) Affiliation: Simular AI
Abstract

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has become a foundation for eliciting multi-step reasoning in large language models, but recent studies show that its benefits do not scale monotonically with chain length: while longer CoT generally enables a model to tackle harder problems, on a given problem, accuracy typically increases with CoT length up to a point, after which it declines. We identify a major cause of this phenomenon: as the CoT grows, the model’s attention to critical insights produced earlier in the trace gradually weakens, making those insights progressively less accessible when they are most needed. Therefore, we propose InsightReplay, a stateful reasoning approach in which the model periodically extracts critical insights from its reasoning trace and replays them near the active generation frontier, keeping them accessible as the reasoning scales. Extensive experiments on a ××𝟒\mathbf{2}\!\times\!\mathbf{3}\!\times\!\mathbf{4} benchmark grid, covering model scales {8B,30B}\{\text{8B},\text{30B}\}, model families {Qwen3.5,DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen,Gemma-4}\{\text{Qwen3.5},\text{DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen},\text{Gemma-4}\}, and reasoning benchmarks {AIME,HMMT,GPQA Diamond,LiveCodeBench v5}\{\text{AIME},\text{HMMT},\text{GPQA Diamond},\text{LiveCodeBench v5}\}, show that 3-round InsightReplay yields accuracy gains across all 24 settings, with an averaged improvement of +1.65\mathbf{+1.65} points over standard CoT, and a largest single-setting gain of +9.2\mathbf{+9.2} points on R1-Distill-32B’s LiveCodeBench v5 subset. Our results suggest that the effectiveness of test-time scaling depends not only on how much a model reasons, but also on whether critical intermediate insights remain accessible throughout long reasoning trajectories.

1 Introduction

Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is a key mechanism for eliciting reasoning in large language models. By explicitly generating intermediate steps, CoT decomposes difficult objectives into smaller sub-problems and has become a foundation for test-time scaling: increasing reasoning-token budgets often improves performance on difficult tasks [1, 2, 3, 4].

However, recent work shows that the benefits of additional reasoning tokens do not scale monotonically. On fixed-difficulty problems, accuracy typically follows an inverted-U relationship with CoT length (see Figure 1): performance first improves as the model reasons longer, reaches a peak, and then declines as the trajectory becomes excessively long [5, 6, 7]. Harder problems shift this peak rightward, requiring longer reasoning before degradation appears.

What drives this decline? Prior work has identified that not all reasoning tokens contribute equally: a small subset of sentences disproportionately determines the final answer, and certain attention heads consistently focus on them [8]. We complement this line of work by asking a different question: how does the model’s access to such critical insights evolve as the reasoning chain grows?

In Section 2.2, we directly measure the pre-softmax attention from answer tokens to critical insights as a function of token distance, and find that it decays monotonically. As a result, later reasoning is conducted with progressively degraded access to the very intermediate conclusions that matter most. This observation suggests a broader view of test-time scaling: increasing reasoning depth alone is insufficient unless important reasoning state can also remain accessible over time.

This echoes a classical challenge in sequence modeling: preserving long-range information across time. LSTM [9] addressed this by introducing an explicit memory cell that persists and is continually updated as the sequence unfolds. A natural question therefore arises for long reasoning chains: can we equip the growing reasoning chain with an analogous mechanism that keeps critical insights accessible over time?

To answer this question, we introduce stateful reasoning for CoT, where the reasoning state at any point is the cumulative set of insights the model has generated so far, compressed abstractions of prior reasoning. We instantiate this with InsightReplay, which periodically generates new insights and replays them near the active generation frontier. Keeping insights close to the decoding position preserves the model’s attention to them. This mitigates the attention decay that critical intermediate content suffers in long trajectories, raising the achievable peak accuracy and expanding the regime in which extended reasoning translates into higher accuracy.

Figure 1 previews this property. The Baseline curve exhibits the characteristic inverted-U pattern: accuracy first rises with CoT length, peaks at around 1515K tokens, and then declines as the chain grows further. InsightReplay behaves differently. It operates precisely in the long CoT regime where additional reasoning already degrades the Baseline, yet each additional replay round (11, 33, 55) achieves progressively higher mean accuracy. By 33 replay rounds, InsightReplay’s mean accuracy already exceeds the Baseline’s peak; by 55 rounds, performance continues to improve further. In effect, InsightReplay turns the Baseline’s degradation regime into a continued-growth regime, extending the range of token budgets over which additional reasoning remains productive.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We empirically study critical insights in CoT and identify two key properties: (I) critical insights and the surrounding reasoning trace are complementary; (II) attention to critical insights decays as CoT grows, making them progressively less accessible to the model.

  • •

    Building on these observations, we propose InsightReplay, a stateful reasoning approach that periodically extracts critical insights and replays them near the active generation frontier. We further provide a theoretical analysis showing that InsightReplay can shift the optimal reasoning length rightward and raise the achievable peak accuracy.

  • •

    We validate InsightReplay in a purely inference-time setting and show that replaying critical insights yields consistent improvements across a broad range of models and reasoning benchmarks, without any additional training.

  • •

    We further reinforce this reasoning pattern through post-training, demonstrating that InsightReplay improves both training stability and reasoning performance over vanilla CoT under same training settings.

2 Properties of Critical Insights in Long CoT

2.1 Critical Insights and the Reasoning Trace are Complementary

Related Work.

Recent work provides evidence that information in CoT is not uniformly distributed: compression methods show that many reasoning tokens can be pruned with minimal accuracy loss [10, 11, 12, 13]; summarize-and-restart methods first generate a reasoning segment, then summarizes it into a compact form, discards the original segment, and resumes thinking from the summary [14, 15, 16]; and importance-attribution methods identify a small number of sentences or tokens that disproportionately influence the final answer [8, 17]. What remains underexplored is the relationship between the original insights produced within the CoT and the surrounding reasoning trace that produced them. We seek to verify and quantify whether the two are substitutable or complementary.

Experimental Setting.

Using Qwen3-8B as the base model, we generate thinking traces for 6060 AIME competition problems [18], with a maximum generation length of 30,00030{,}000 tokens. We then use the same model to extract 55–77 key insights from each trace. We construct seven conditions with identical chat templates and answer formats, differing only in the content inside the thinking tag: (A) original full thinking; (B) repeated question + insights; (C) insights only; (D) full thinking + repeated question + insights; (E) full thinking + insights; (F) random tokens + repeated question + insights; (G) random tokens + insights. For each condition, we compute the answer probability P⁡(ans):=Pθ​(agt∣x)=∏tPθ​(agt(t)∣x,agt(<t))P(\mathrm{ans}):=P_{\theta}(a_{\mathrm{gt}}\mid x)=\prod_{t}P_{\theta}(a_{\mathrm{gt}}^{(t)}\mid x,a_{\mathrm{gt}}^{(<t)}) via a single forward pass on Qwen3-8B, where xx is the prompt prefix up to and including \boxed{ and agta_{\mathrm{gt}} are the ground-truth answer tokens; full details are in Appendix A.

Results & Conclusion.

Table 1 reveals four observations: (I) Insights carry concentrated signal. Condition C retains 75.6%75.6\% of the answer probability with only 1.4%1.4\% of the tokens, indicating that the core reasoning content distills into a small set of critical insights. (II) Insights provide additive value on top of the reasoning trace. Replaying insights on top of the original reasoning trace further improves accuracy from 0.5120.512 to 0.5450.545–0.5570.557, demonstrating that even when the reasoning trace is already present, re-exposing the model to its own insights yields measurable gains. (III) Bad reasoning trace actively harms inference. As an extreme case, F and G replace the entire CoT reasoning trace with length-matched random tokens, dropping accuracy to 0.1270.127–0.1310.131, which is below the insight-only conditions B (0.2730.273) and C (0.3870.387). (IV) Repeating the question helps only when paired with a reasoning trace. The repeated question helps with a real reasoning trace (D vs. E), but hurts substantially without any reasoning trace (B vs. C).

2.2 Critical Insights Become Less Accessible as Reasoning Chains Grow

Related Work.

While prior work has identified important reasoning steps and the heads that attend to them [8], and while positional encodings such as RoPE [19] are known to bias attention toward nearby tokens, empirical attention patterns are ultimately shaped by learned query-key interactions rather than positional geometry alone [20]. Whether attention to critical insights actually decays with distance therefore requires direct measurement. We take critical insights as the unit of analysis and measure how attention from answer tokens to these insights varies with token distance.

Experimental Setting.

On 6060 AIME problems with Qwen3-8B and Gemma-4-31B-it, the model first generates a CoT trace, after which Qwen3.5-397B-A17B identifies 55–77 critical insights, each localized to a token span cc ending at position pep_{e}. We use a stronger extractor here because attention measurement requires precise token boundaries that smaller models do not produce reliably. To isolate the effect of distance, we insert semantically neutral filler tokens at sentence boundaries between the insight and the answer. Each filler unit is "\n " (newline + space), chosen for its minimal semantic impact. Let pap_{a} denote the answer position, so the baseline distance is d=pa−ped=p_{a}-p_{e}. We sweep an insertion ratio ρ∈{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4}\rho\in\{0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4\}, inserting N=⌊ρ​d⌋N=\lfloor\rho d\rfloor filler units total, distributed uniformly at random across the sentence boundaries between insight and answer. The resulting total distance is (1+ρ)​d(1+\rho)d regardless of placement. We use one sample at ρ=0\rho=0 and 1010 random allocations at each non-zero ρ\rho, yielding 4141 variants per insight. Since the insight and all preceding tokens are untouched, any change in attention is primarily attributable to distance. For each variant, we compute the per-layer pre-softmax attention score from the answer token to the insight span:

s(ℓ)​(c,a)=1|H|​∑h1|c|​∑t∈c𝐪pa(ℓ,h)⋅𝐤t(ℓ,h)dhead,s^{(\ell)}(c,a)\;=\;\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h}\;\frac{1}{|c|}\sum_{t\in c}\;\frac{\mathbf{q}_{p_{a}}^{(\ell,h)}\cdot\mathbf{k}_{t}^{(\ell,h)}}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}},

where cc denotes the set of token positions covered by the insight span (with |c||c| its size and tt ranging over its elements), ℓ\ell is the layer index, hh indexes attention heads, 𝐪\mathbf{q} and 𝐤\mathbf{k} are post-RoPE query and key vectors, |H||H| is the number of heads, and dheadd_{\mathrm{head}} is the per-head dimension. We use pre-softmax scores rather than post-softmax weights because softmax normalization over the full preceding context mechanically squashes weights as context length grows, confounding the effect of distance with that of sequence length. Full implementation details are in Appendix B.

Results & Conclusion

Figure 2 reports the relative decline in attention to critical insights from ρ=0\rho{=}0 to ρ=0.4\rho{=}0.4: 19.2%19.2\% for Qwen3-8B (final layer) and 3.3%3.3\% for Gemma-4-31B-it (final global-attention layer). We draw two conclusions: (I) Within each model, attention to critical insights decays monotonically as the insight is pushed away from the generation frontier, and the decline is highly significant (p<0.001p<0.001). (II) The decay is not specific to a single architecture or RoPE configuration: it persists in Gemma-4-31B-it, which uses partial-rotary RoPE on only the first quarter of head dimensions and a different attention scaling, suggesting the phenomenon reflects a general property of trained attention rather than a feature of any specific positional encoding.

3 InsightReplay

3.1 Method Overview

Figure 3 illustrates the core idea of InsightReplay. Reasoning unfolds as an interleaving of two types of content: reasoning chunks (RtR_{t}), in which the model performs step-by-step thinking, and insights (ItI_{t}), short distilled conclusions the model itself produces to summarize prior reasoning. As the trajectory progresses, the sequence of insights {It}\{I_{t}\} acts as a continuously updated, compressed abstraction of what has been concluded so far, kept near the active generation frontier so it remains accessible to subsequent reasoning. One specific example is shown in Appendix D.6.

Method Description.

The process begins from the user question QQ. We initialize I0=QI_{0}\!=\!Q, treating the question itself as a “goal insight” that anchors all subsequent reasoning, consistent with Section 2.1. The model then enters a periodic loop. At each round tt, conditioned on the full history (Q,R1,I1,…,Rt−1,It−1)(Q,R_{1},I_{1},\ldots,R_{t-1},I_{t-1}), the model: (i) generates a reasoning chunk RtR_{t}, and (ii) generates a new insight ItI_{t} via a summarization prompt that asks the model to consolidate the conclusions reached so far, with the thinking content R1,…,RtR_{1},\ldots,R_{t} retained in context. Both RtR_{t} and ItI_{t} are appended to the history in order. Crucially, because ItI_{t} is generated in the presence of all prior insights I0,…,It−1I_{0},\ldots,I_{t-1}, each new insight can reflect on and supersede earlier ones—incorporating new conclusions, correcting prior errors, or refining imprecise statements. The cumulative trace of insights thus forms an evolving abstraction of the reasoning so far, rather than a flat concatenation of independent summaries. After NN rounds (a hyperparameter; we ablate N∈{1,3}N\!\in\!\{1,3\} in Section 4), the model produces the final answer AA from the complete history. By construction, the most recent It−1I_{t-1} always sits immediately before RtR_{t}, keeping the latest distilled conclusions close to the decoding position of subsequent reasoning.

3.2 Theoretical Analysis

In this section, we formalize the observations from Sections 2.1 and 2.2, and prove that InsightReplay provably shifts the optimal CoT length rightward and raises the peak accuracy.

3.2.1 Modeling

Following Wu et al. [5], for a task qq with difficulty TT and model θ\theta, the probability of an NN-step CoT producing the correct final answer is:

P⁡(afinal|q,θ,N)=∏i=1NP⁡(qi|Hi−1,q,θ,N)⏟sub-question​P⁡(ai|qi,Hi−1,q,θ,N)⏟sub-answer,P(a_{\mathrm{final}}|q,\theta,N)=\prod_{i=1}^{N}\underbrace{P(q_{i}|H_{i-1},q,\theta,N)}_{\text{sub-question}}\;\underbrace{P(a_{i}|q_{i},H_{i-1},q,\theta,N)}_{\text{sub-answer}}, (1)

where Hk:=[t1,a1,…,tk,ak]H_{k}:=[t_{1},a_{1},\dots,t_{k},a_{k}] denotes the reasoning history up to step kk.

They parameterize the sub-question accuracy as (1−σ⁡(T))(1-\sigma(T)), where σ⁡(T)\sigma(T) denotes the probability that the model fails to generate the correct next sub-question for a task of total difficulty TT, and the sub-answer accuracy as (1−E⁡(N,M,T))(1-E(N,M,T)) with a linear error model E⁡(N,M,T)=T/(N​M)E(N,M,T)=T/(NM), where MM represents the model’s reasoning capability. Thus, the accuracy of NN-step reasoning is:

A0​(N)=α​[(1−σ⁡(T))​(1−T/(N​M))]N,A_{0}(N)=\alpha\,\bigl[(1-\sigma(T))(1-T/(NM))\bigr]^{N}, (2)

where α\alpha is a constant independent of NN. Crucially, their parameterization drops the dependence on the history Hi−1H_{i-1}, implicitly assuming each step’s accuracy is independent of its position in the chain.

However, our Section 2.2 shows: as ii increases, the model’s ability to access critical insights from earlier steps diminishes due to attention decay. We restore this missing dependence by introducing an insight accessibility function Φ⁡(i)\Phi(i) into the sub-question term. Specifically, we model the sub-question accuracy at step ii as (1−σ⁡(T))⋅Φ⁡(i)(1-\sigma(T))\cdot\Phi(i), where Φ⁡(i)\Phi(i) captures how effectively the model can access prior insights when formulating the ii-th sub-question. We apply Φ⁡(i)\Phi(i) to the sub-question term because generating the correct next sub-question requires synthesizing prior insights, whereas answering a sub-question, once correctly posed, depends primarily on the sub-question itself.

Assumption 1.

The insight accessibility function Φ:[0,∞)→(0,1]\Phi:[0,\infty)\to(0,1] satisfies:

  1. 1.

    Φ⁡(0)=1\Phi(0)=1 (zero distance ⇒\Rightarrow full accessibility);

  2. 2.

    Φ\Phi is strictly monotonically decreasing (Section 2.2) (farther ⇒\Rightarrow less accessible);

  3. 3.

    limi→∞Φ⁡(i)=0\displaystyle\lim_{i\to\infty}\Phi(i)=0 (infinite distance ⇒\Rightarrow inaccessible).

Under this modeling, we define two accuracy functions:

Real-world CoT vs. InsightReplay.

We define two accuracy functions, where p⁡(N):=(1−σ⁡(T))​(1−E⁡(N,M,T))p(N):=(1-\sigma(T))(1-E(N,M,T)) denotes the per-step accuracy without decay. The real-world CoT accuracy AΦA_{\Phi} accounts for insight decay via Φ⁡(i)\Phi(i), while InsightReplay relocates critical insights to a fixed distance d0≥0d_{0}\geq 0 from the generation frontier at every step, replacing Φ⁡(i)\Phi(i) with the constant Φ⁡(d0)\Phi(d_{0}):

AΦ​(N)=[p⁡(N)]N​∏i=1NΦ⁡(i),AIR​(N)=[p⁡(N)⋅Φ⁡(d0)]N.A_{\Phi}(N)=[p(N)]^{N}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Phi(i),\qquad A_{\mathrm{IR}}(N)=[p(N)\cdot\Phi(d_{0})]^{N}. (3)

We first state two structural lemmas that underlie our main results. Let g⁡(N):=dd​N​[N​ln⁡p⁡(N)]g(N):=\frac{d}{dN}[N\ln p(N)].

Lemma 1 (Strict concavity).

ln⁡A0​(N)\ln A_{0}(N) is strictly concave for N>T/MN>T/M, and consequently gg is strictly decreasing on this domain.

Lemma 2 (Uniqueness of optima).

AΦA_{\Phi} and AIRA_{\mathrm{IR}} each admit a unique maximizer on (0,∞)(0,\infty), characterized by

g⁡(NΦ∗)=−ln⁡Φ⁡(NΦ∗),g⁡(NIR∗)=−ln⁡Φ⁡(d0).g(N_{\Phi}^{*})=-\ln\Phi(N_{\Phi}^{*}),\qquad g(N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*})=-\ln\Phi(d_{0}). (4)

Theorem 1 (InsightReplay shifts the optimal length rightward).

NIR∗>NΦ∗N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*}>N_{\Phi}^{*}.

Theorem 1 follows because InsightReplay places insights adjacent to the generation frontier (d0≪NΦ∗d_{0}\ll N_{\Phi}^{*}), so Φ⁡(d0)>Φ⁡(NΦ∗)\Phi(d_{0})>\Phi(N_{\Phi}^{*}). Full proofs are deferred to Appendix C.

4 Pure Inference Experiments

We evaluate InsightReplay across a 2×3×42\times 3\times 4 experimental grid: two model scales, three model families, and four reasoning benchmarks. Full implementation details are provided in Appendix D.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Models.

We evaluate 66 open-weight reasoning models, organized into a 2×32\times 3 grid of scales and families: (1) Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B [21], where the latter is a mixture-of-experts model with 33B active parameters; (2) Gemma-4-E4B and Gemma-4-31B-it [22], dense models that interleave local sliding-window attention (10241024 tokens) with global full-context attention and apply partial-rotary RoPE on the first quarter of head dimensions in global layers; (3) R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and R1-Distill-Qwen-32B [3], distilled from DeepSeek-R1 onto Qwen2.5 backbones.

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on four reasoning benchmarks: AIME 2025/2026 [18] (60 math problems with integer answers), HMMT [23] (60 Harvard–MIT competition math problems), GPQA Diamond [24] (198 graduate-level science MCQs), and LiveCodeBench v5 [25] (62 code problems uniformly sampled from the full benchmark; see Appendix D for the sampling procedure).

Variants.

We compare four inference variants: (1) Base: standard thinking-mode CoT; (2) VO (Verify-Only): the model is prompted to continue thinking after its initial trace via a budget-forcing cue ("Wait, let me double-check..."), but performs no insight extraction or replay; (3) IR1 / (4) IR3: InsightReplay with 1 or 3 rounds of extract-then-replay. The contrast between IRkk and VO isolates the contribution of the InsightReplay mechanism beyond extended thinking alone.

Sampling and metrics.

For each problem, we draw 1616 completions with temperature τ=1\tau=1 and top-p=0.95p=0.95. The model generates until it produces an EOS token or reaches its native context length. We report accuracy as the primary metric, with average completion tokens as a cost measure.

4.2 Main Results

Table 2 summarizes the results.

InsightReplay improves accuracy across all 2424 settings.

IR3 yields strictly non-negative gains on every cell, with macro-averaged improvement of +1.65+1.65 points and micro-averaged improvement of +1.21+1.21 points over Base. The largest gains are observed on R1-Distill-32B/LCB (+9.2+9.2); the smallest are on settings already close to ceiling, such as Qwen3.5-35B/HMMT (+0.1+0.1).

Gains are not merely an artifact of extended thinking.

VO instructs the model to keep thinking after its initial trace but performs no insight extraction; despite using comparable token budgets, VO captures only +0.61+0.61 of the macro-averaged gain. The remaining +1.04+1.04, captured by IR3 over VO, is attributable to the InsightReplay mechanism itself. In other words, more than 60%60\% of the total improvement comes from insight extraction and replay rather than from additional thinking time.

Token overhead is moderate.

IR3 consumes on average 1.36×1.36\times the tokens of Base, reflecting the insight extraction and replay rounds; IR1 incurs only 1.14×1.14\times overhead while still delivering a macro-averaged improvement of +0.90+0.90. Given the consistent accuracy gains across 2424 settings, many of which involve baselines already near saturation, this represents a favorable accuracy–cost trade-off.

Agentic Evaluation.

We additionally evaluate InsightReplay in an agentic setting on SWE-Bench-Verified [26]. Due to space constraints, we defer the full protocol and results to Appendix E.

4.3 Empirical Validation of Peak Accuracy

We test the prediction of Theorem 2: InsightReplay should raise the achievable peak accuracy. We reuse the samples collected for the main results. For each problem, we sort the 1616 Baseline completions by token count and bin them into 88 length levels (two samples per level). Binning is performed within each problem rather than globally to avoid conflating length with difficulty: a global short bin would be dominated by easy problems. The VO/IR1/IR3 samples inherit the bin assignment of their parent Baseline, so all variants are compared within each length level on samples sharing the same Baseline starting points. The Baseline curve in Figure 4 reports per-bin accuracy averaged over the four benchmarks (88 data points). For each of VO, IR1, and IR3, we compute per-bin accuracy under the same binning protocol and report the peak across the 88 bins, shown as a single star marker. See details in Appendix F. To probe whether the trend extrapolates beyond the ablated range, we additionally run IR5 on the LiveCodeBench v5 subset; the result is reported in Figure 1.

Figure 4 reports the curves for the three ∼30\sim 30B-scale models. We highlight two findings.

The peak accuracy rises.

The IR3 peak exceeds the Base peak on all models: 86.06%→86.83%86.06\%\!\to\!86.83\% on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, 88.25%→89.13%88.25\%\!\to\!89.13\% on Gemma-4-31B-it, and 50.51%→53.48%50.51\%\!\to\!53.48\% on R1-Distill-32B. This matches Theorem 2 that the same mitigation also lifts the achievable peak.

Test-time scaling alone is insufficient.

Budget-forced thinking alone fails to lift the peak. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, VO’s peak is below Base. The peak rise is therefore driven primarily by the InsightReplay mechanism rather than extended thinking alone.

5 Post-Training Experiments

To study whether InsightReplay can be reinforced through RL, we train Qwen3-4B-Base [27] with GRPO, comparing InsightReplay-enabled rollouts against standard CoT rollouts.

Setup.

We use GRPO [28] as the policy-optimization algorithm and adopt the DAPO [29] soft overlong reward shaping to stabilize long-CoT training. The actor is trained on DAPO-Math-15K [29] with a maximum response length of 30,72030{,}720 tokens, a rollout group size of 88 per prompt, and a global batch size of 256256 prompts. Validation is performed on AIME 2025 every 2020 training steps with n=32n{=}32 samples per problem, from which we report best​@​32\mathrm{best@32}, maj​@​32\mathrm{maj@32}, and mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32}. Both runs use the same base model, data, and random seed. Full hyperparameters are provided in Appendix G.

Rollout Protocol.

The two settings differ only in how rollouts are generated. In the Baseline setting, the policy generates a single thinking trace until it emits the EOS token or reaches the maximum response length. In the InsightReplay setting, once the policy emits the EOS token, we append a fixed continuation cue asking the model to extract and replay the insights (exact text in Appendix G). Generation then continues under the same length budget, so the total response length matches the baseline exactly. The cue is inserted with response​_​mask=0\mathrm{response\_mask}{=}0 which isolates the effect of the InsightReplay reasoning pattern from any auxiliary supervision signal.

Alternative Training Designs.

We also experimented with a more elaborate scheme that explicitly encodes the multi-round InsightReplay structure during training via a 2D attention mask combined with per-round trace bundling. While methodologically clean, this design costs more compute than the protocol above. Nonetheless, we document this attempt in Appendix H for the interested reader.

Results.

Figure 5 reveals three observations comparing InsightReplay against the baseline.

(1) Training stability. The standard CoT baseline exhibits a pronounced late-training degradation: after step 300300, all three metrics decline. The mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32} drops from a peak of 27.9%27.9\% at step 280280 to 21.6%21.6\% at step 560560; best​@​32\mathrm{best@32} similarly decays from 57.5%57.5\% at step 280280 to 42.0%42.0\% at step 620620. In contrast, InsightReplay maintains stable performance throughout training: from step 200200 onward, mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32} stays within the 25.0%25.0\%–29.0%29.0\% band, with no monotonic decline observed up to step 600600.

(2) Peak accuracy. InsightReplay also achieves higher peak validation accuracy across all three metrics. On maj​@​32\mathrm{maj@32}, InsightReplay peaks at 38.8%38.8\% versus 34.1%34.1\% for the baseline, an absolute improvement of +4.7+4.7 points; on mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32}, 28.8%28.8\%versus 27.9%27.9\%, a gain of +0.9+0.9 points; and on best​@​32\mathrm{best@32}, 59.1%59.1\% versus 57.5%57.5\%, a gain of +1.6+1.6 points. The peak gap is most pronounced on maj​@​32\mathrm{maj@32}, which aggregates evidence across the 3232 samples and is therefore most sensitive to whether the underlying reasoning is consistent suggesting that InsightReplay improves the distribution of outputs.

(3) The advantage is not an initialization effect.  For the first ∼200\sim 200 steps, the two methods’ learning curves overlap within sampling noise on all three metrics; divergence emerges only after step ∼250\sim 250. This rules out alternative explanations such as the InsightReplay prompt placing the policy in a more favorable starting region or its reward shape biasing the optimization from the outset. The benefit must be produced during training rather than inherited from the setup.

Together, the three observations show that the InsightReplay reasoning pattern can be reinforced through RL training rather than only used at inference time. Beyond improving peak accuracy, it stabilizes long-CoT GRPO training in a regime where the standard CoT baseline suffers a pronounced late-training degradation, and does so without relying on any early-learning advantage. This positions InsightReplay as a reasoning pattern compatible with both inference-time and training-time use.

6 Limitation

Although InsightReplay can deliver substantial absolute gains where the base model has substantive room to grow, with the largest single-cell improvement reaching +9.2+9.2 points on R1-Distill-32B/LiveCodeBench v5 subset(lifting 25.8%25.8\% to 35.0%35.0\%, +35.7%+35.7\% relative), the gains are bounded by each benchmark’s available headroom. On near-saturated settings the marginal improvement is modest: on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B/HMMT, IR3 improves over an 88.5%88.5\% baseline by only +0.1+0.1 points. This pattern is consistent with our theoretical framework, in which Φ⁡(d0)\Phi(d_{0}) relocation cannot exceed the ceiling imposed by p⁡(N)p(N) itself. We therefore expect InsightReplay to provide the largest practical value on hard reasoning tasks where the underlying model is far from saturation.

7 Conclusion

We introduced InsightReplay, a stateful reasoning approach that periodically extracts critical insights from the CoT trace and replays them near the active generation frontier. By mitigating the attention decay that critical insights suffer in long trajectories, InsightReplay reshapes the inverted-U between CoT length and accuracy, shifting the peak rightward and lifting it upward, thereby expanding the regime in which extended reasoning translates into higher accuracy. We support this through both theoretical analysis and empirical validation: positive gains across all 2424 cells of our scale ×\times family ×\times benchmark grid in the pure-inference setting, and consistent improvements in training stability and peak accuracy when used as a rollout protocol for post-training.

Appendix A Experimental Details for Property I

Dataset.

We use 6060 problems from the American Invitational Mathematics Examination (AIME) spanning the 20242024 and 20252025 competitions.

Thinking trace generation.

For each problem, we generate 1616 independent chain-of-thought samples using Qwen3-8B in its native thinking mode, and report results averaged over these samples. We use the Qwen3 chat template and prompt the model with:

Solve the following math competition problem step by step. Show your detailed reasoning, then give your final answer as a single integer inside \boxed{}.

Generation is performed via vLLM [30] with sampling (temperature=0.6{}=0.6, top_p=0.95{}=0.95), tensor parallelism across 22 GPUs, max_model_len=30,000{}=30{,}000, dtype=bfloat16, and a maximum of 30,00030{,}000 new tokens. The model’s output follows the <think>...</think> convention; we parse the content inside the tags as the thinking trace and the content outside as the final response. For traces that reach the 30,00030{,}000-token limit before producing a closing </think> tag, we treat the content up to the closing tag as the thinking trace if it appears, and otherwise treat the entire generated output as the thinking trace. All seven conditions in Section 2.1 are evaluated on the same set of 60×16=96060\times 16=960 generated traces.

Insight extraction.

For each thinking trace, we use Qwen3-8B to extract a list of 55–77 key insights. The extraction model receives the original question and the full thinking trace, and is instructed to:

Extract exactly 55 to 77 key insights from this thinking, in the order they were derived. Each insight should be one concrete sentence containing specific numbers, equations, or results—not vague descriptions.

The model produces a numbered list (e.g. 1. The area of △​A​B​C\triangle ABC is 6​146\sqrt{14} by Heron’s formula.), which we parse with a regex-based extractor that captures each enumerated entry. We cap the result at 77 insights per problem in the rare cases where the model produces more. This phase uses vLLM with greedy decoding, max_tokens=8192{}=8192, and the same tensor parallelism configuration as the trace generation phase. Across all 6060 problems and 1616 samples per problem, the mean number of extracted insights is 6.96.9, with all extractions falling within the requested 55–77 range.

Probability scoring.

We load Qwen3-8B via HuggingFace Transformers in bfloat16 precision on a single GPU. For each problem, we construct a prefix string following the Qwen3 chat template:

<|im_start|>user
{user_prompt}<|im_end|>
<|im_start|>assistant
<think>
{THINK_CONTENT}
</think>

\boxed{

where THINK_CONTENT varies across conditions (see below). We then append the ground-truth answer tokens agt=(a1,a2,…,aK)a_{\mathrm{gt}}=(a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{K}) (the tokenized integer answer) to the prefix and perform a single forward pass over the concatenated sequence. The score is the joint log-probability of the answer tokens conditioned on the prefix:

log⁡Pθ​(agt∣xprefix)=∑k=1Klog⁡Pθ​(ak∣xprefix,a<k),\log P_{\theta}(a_{\mathrm{gt}}\mid x_{\mathrm{prefix}})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\log P_{\theta}\!\bigl(a_{k}\mid x_{\mathrm{prefix}},a_{<k}\bigr), (5)

where xprefixx_{\mathrm{prefix}} denotes the prompt up to and including the opening token sequence \boxed{, and KK is the number of tokens in the tokenized ground-truth answer.

Condition definitions.

Let 𝐪\mathbf{q} denote the problem statement, 𝐭\mathbf{t} the full thinking trace generated in the previous paragraph, and 𝐟=(f1,…,fK)\mathbf{f}=(f_{1},\dots,f_{K}) the insights extracted by the extraction step (formatted as a numbered list). Let 𝐫\mathbf{r} denote a sequence of pseudo-random tokens whose token count matches that of 𝐭\mathbf{t} for the same problem. The seven conditions differ only in THINK_CONTENT:

  • (A)

    Full thinking (baseline): 𝐭\mathbf{t}

  • (B)

    Repeated question + insights: Question: 𝐪\mathbf{q}, followed by 𝐟\mathbf{f}

  • (C)

    Insights only: 𝐟\mathbf{f}

  • (D)

    Full thinking + repeated question + insights: 𝐭\mathbf{t}, then Question: 𝐪\mathbf{q}, followed by 𝐟\mathbf{f}

  • (E)

    Full thinking + insights: 𝐭\mathbf{t}, followed by 𝐟\mathbf{f}

  • (F)

    Random tokens + repeated question + insights: 𝐫\mathbf{r}, then Question: 𝐪\mathbf{q}, followed by 𝐟\mathbf{f}

  • (G)

    Random tokens + insights: 𝐫\mathbf{r}, followed by 𝐟\mathbf{f}

Adjacent components are concatenated with two newline characters (\n\n). To construct 𝐫\mathbf{r}, we sample strings of the form xq{0--9999} with a fixed random seed of 4242 for reproducibility, then truncate or pad at the token level to match |tokenize⁡(𝐭)||\mathrm{tokenize}(\mathbf{t})| exactly.

Software and hardware.

All experiments use vLLM 0.19.00.19.0 for trace generation and insight extraction, and HuggingFace Transformers 5.6.05.6.0 for probability scoring. Models are served in bfloat16 precision. Trace generation and insight extraction each run on 2×2{\times} NVIDIA GPUs with tensor parallelism; probability scoring runs on a single GPU.

Appendix B Experimental Details for Property II

Models.

Qwen3-8B: 36 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads via GQA, head dim 128128, full RoPE, with QK-norm. Gemma-4-31B-it: alternates sliding-window and global-attention layers with different head dimensions and per-layer partial_rotary_factor; we extract scores only from global layers (head_dim =512=512) so the attention pattern is not truncated by the sliding window. The insight-extraction model is Qwen3.5-397B-A17B.

CoT generation.

Each target model generates a complete CoT trace via vLLM with greedy decoding (max_new_tokens==38,000, temperature==1.0, do_sample==False, bfloat16). The user prompt is:

Solve the following math problem step by step. Show your complete reasoning, then give the final answer inside \boxed{}.

For Qwen3-8B we wrap the trace in <think>...</think>; for Gemma-4 we use the native thought block. The ground-truth answer is appended as \boxed{<answer>} at the fixed position pap_{a} (the first token after \boxed{).

Insight extraction and token-level localization.

We prompt Qwen3.5-397B-A17B to list 55–77 critical insights, each containing a verbatim span copied from the trace. Each insight is then relocated in the full tokenized sequence via a case-sensitive substring match plus character-to-token offset mapping using the target model’s tokenizer, yielding (start_token_idx, end_token_idx) for the insight span cc. Insights whose verbatim span cannot be recovered, or whose sentence position leaves fewer than one downstream sentence before pap_{a}, are discarded. This yields an average of ∼6{\sim}6 usable insights per problem.

Filler unit calibration.

The filler unit "\n " is calibrated per tokenizer at runtime to determine its token cost τ\tau. The number of filler units actually inserted at ratio ρ\rho is N=⌊⌊ρ⋅d⌋/τ⌋N=\lfloor\lfloor\rho\cdot d\rfloor/\tau\rfloor, and the realized distance after insertion is d′=d+N⋅τd^{\prime}=d+N\cdot\tau. Random allocation of fillers across sentence boundaries uses a seeded RNG (seed==42 plus problem-id hash) for reproducibility.

Attention-score extraction.

We run a layer-by-layer forward pass with bfloat16. At each layer ℓ\ell we recompute the post-RoPE query vector 𝐪pa(ℓ,h)\mathbf{q}^{(\ell,h)}_{p_{a}} and post-RoPE key vectors 𝐤t(ℓ,h)\mathbf{k}^{(\ell,h)}_{t} for t∈ct\in c, and store the per-layer score s(ℓ)​(c,a)s^{(\ell)}(c,a) together with the realized distance d′d^{\prime}. For GQA models we map each query head to its shared KV head via integer division by the GQA group size.

Model-specific handling.

Qwen3-8B applies standard full-dimension RoPE and QK-norm; we replicate the ordering q-proj →\to q-norm →\to RoPE, and likewise for keys. Gemma-4-31B-it uses head_dim =512=512 on global layers; to avoid materializing the full attention matrix at this size we use PyTorch SDPA for head_dim>>256 and fall back to flash_attention_2 elsewhere. Only the explicit 𝐪⋅𝐤\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} computation for the (answer, insight) pair enters the logging path.

Aggregation and reporting.

Scores are aggregated per (ℓ,ρ)(\ell,\rho) by first averaging across samples, then across insights within a problem, then across problems. For distance-based plots, we bin by realized distance d′d^{\prime} with bin size 500500 tokens. We additionally identify candidate “receiver” heads as the top-3232 heads ranked by score kurtosis across variants.

Compute.

Attention extraction uses 88-way data parallelism across NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each worker loads one full model instance (Qwen3-8B on one GPU; Gemma-4-31B-it sharded across multiple GPUs via device_map). All intermediate artifacts (CoTs, insights, token locations, variants, raw scores) are persisted to JSONL/CSV and released with the code.

We prove the claim for AΦA_{\Phi}; the argument for AIRA_{\mathrm{IR}} is analogous. On the meaningful domain N>T/MN>T/M, as N→(T/M)+N\to(T/M)^{+}, g⁡(N)→+∞g(N)\to+\infty while ln⁡Φ⁡(N)\ln\Phi(N) remains finite, so (ln⁡AΦ)′​(N)=g⁡(N)+ln⁡Φ⁡(N)→+∞>0(\ln A_{\Phi})^{\prime}(N)=g(N)+\ln\Phi(N)\to+\infty>0. As N→∞N\to\infty, g⁡(N)→ln⁡(1−σ)<0g(N)\to\ln(1-\sigma)<0 and ln⁡Φ⁡(N)→−∞\ln\Phi(N)\to-\infty, so (ln⁡AΦ)′​(N)→−∞<0(\ln A_{\Phi})^{\prime}(N)\to-\infty<0. By the intermediate value theorem, a critical point exists. Since g⁡(N)g(N) is strictly decreasing (Lemma 1) and −ln⁡Φ⁡(N)-\ln\Phi(N) is strictly increasing (Assumption 1), the optimality condition g⁡(N)=−ln⁡Φ⁡(N)g(N)=-\ln\Phi(N) has at most one solution, so the maximizer is unique. ∎

C.2 Main Results

C.2.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof.

By design, InsightReplay places the relocated insight adjacent to the active generation frontier, so d0≪NΦ∗d_{0}\ll N_{\Phi}^{*} in any meaningful regime. Combined with the strict monotonicity of Φ\Phi (Assumption 1), this yields Φ⁡(d0)>Φ⁡(NΦ∗)\Phi(d_{0})>\Phi(N_{\Phi}^{*}), and hence −ln⁡Φ⁡(d0)<−ln⁡Φ⁡(NΦ∗)-\ln\Phi(d_{0})<-\ln\Phi(N_{\Phi}^{*}). By the optimality conditions in Eq. (13), g⁡(NΦ∗)=−ln⁡Φ⁡(NΦ∗)g(N_{\Phi}^{*})=-\ln\Phi(N_{\Phi}^{*}) and g⁡(NIR∗)=−ln⁡Φ⁡(d0)g(N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*})=-\ln\Phi(d_{0}), so g⁡(NIR∗)<g⁡(NΦ∗)g(N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*})<g(N_{\Phi}^{*}). Since gg is strictly decreasing (Eq. (9)), this implies NIR∗>NΦ∗N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*}>N_{\Phi}^{*}. ∎

C.2.2 Proof of Theorem 2

Proof.

Assume d0<1d_{0}<1 (InsightReplay places the insight within less than one step’s distance). Then for all i≥1i\geq 1, since Φ\Phi is strictly decreasing (Assumption 1, condition 2), Φ⁡(d0)>Φ⁡(i)\Phi(d_{0})>\Phi(i). Therefore, for any N≥1N\geq 1:

AIR​(N)=[p⁡(N)]N⋅[Φ⁡(d0)]N>[p⁡(N)]N⋅∏i=1NΦ⁡(i)=AΦ​(N).A_{\mathrm{IR}}(N)=[p(N)]^{N}\cdot[\Phi(d_{0})]^{N}>[p(N)]^{N}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Phi(i)=A_{\Phi}(N). (14)

In particular, at N=NΦ∗N=N_{\Phi}^{*}: AIR​(NΦ∗)>AΦ​(NΦ∗)A_{\mathrm{IR}}(N_{\Phi}^{*})>A_{\Phi}(N_{\Phi}^{*}). Since NIR∗N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*} maximizes AIRA_{\mathrm{IR}}:

AIR​(NIR∗)≥AIR​(NΦ∗)>AΦ​(NΦ∗).A_{\mathrm{IR}}(N_{\mathrm{IR}}^{*})\geq A_{\mathrm{IR}}(N_{\Phi}^{*})>A_{\Phi}(N_{\Phi}^{*}). (15)

∎

Appendix D Pure Inference Experiment Details

This appendix expands on the experimental setup of Section 4, covering inference infrastructure, decoding configuration, prompting templates, evaluation protocol, and reproducibility notes that were omitted from the main text for brevity.

D.1 Hardware and Inference Stack

All inference experiments are run on a single node with 8×8\times NVIDIA H200 141GB GPUs interconnected via NVLink. Models are served through vLLM [30] v0.19.00.19.0 via its OpenAI-compatible HTTP endpoint, with one server instance per model and all 88 GPUs visible to that instance. The parallelism layout depends on model size: the 30B-tier models (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-31B-it, R1-Distill-Qwen-32B) use tensor parallelism TP=2\text{TP}=2 with data parallelism DP=4\text{DP}=4, while the 8B-tier models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-E4B-it, R1-Distill-Qwen-7B) use TP=1\text{TP}=1 with DP=8\text{DP}=8. KV-cache memory utilization is capped at 0.920.92. The maximum context length is set per model family at the largest value the KV budget can hold under the chosen DP: 200,000200{,}000 tokens for Qwen and Gemma, and the native 131,072131{,}072 tokens for the R1-distill family. We pass --trust-remote-code so that custom model code – e.g. Gemma’s interleaved local/global attention with sliding-window size 10241024 – loads with its released configuration; no custom attention modification is applied on our side.

D.2 Decoding Configuration

We sample with temperature τ=1.0\tau=1.0 and nucleus top-​p=0.95\text{top-}p=0.95; all other vLLM sampling parameters (e.g. top_k, repetition_penalty, presence/frequency penalties) are left at their library defaults so the comparison is not biased by ad-hoc decoding tweaks. We pass skip_special_tokens=False so that thinking-block markers (⟨\langlethink⟩\rangle / ⟨\langle/think⟩\rangle for Qwen and R1-distill, ⟨|\langle|channel⟩\ranglethought / ⟨\langlechannel|⟩|\rangle for Gemma) appear in the raw response; downstream extraction relies on these markers to split the thinking trace from the post-think tail. The k=16k=16 samples per problem are produced by issuing kk independent requests with n=1n=1 rather than a single request with n=kn=k: this guarantees that vLLM’s continuous-batching scheduler treats each sample as an independent unit, and that an HTTP retry on a transient error does not invalidate sibling samples. Independence across samples is provided by vLLM’s internal RNG; no per-sample seed is pinned.

D.3 Prompting Templates

User-turn header.

The user-turn content is a dataset-specific header concatenated with the formatted question; the chat template then wraps it into a model-specific prompt. The header explicitly specifies the answer-format the grader keys on:

  • •

    AIME: “Solve the math problem. Final answer must be a single non-negative integer in ⟨\langleAnswer⟩\rangle…⟨\langle/Answer⟩\rangle.”

  • •

    GPQA Diamond: “Select the best answer. Final answer must be a single letter (A, B, C, or D) in ⟨\langleAnswer⟩\rangle…⟨\langle/Answer⟩\rangle.”

  • •

    LiveCodeBench v5: “Solve the coding task. Put your final solution in a single Python code block delimited by ```python ... ```.”

  • •

    HMMT (Feb & Nov 2025): “Solve the math problem. Final answer must be the EXACT value (simplified, no decimal approximations) in \boxed{...}. If there are multiple solutions, list all of them inside the single \boxed{...} separated by commas.” The boxed-LaTeX format is used (rather than the ⟨\langleAnswer⟩\rangle tag of AIME/GPQA) because HMMT answers are arbitrary symbolic expressions (e.g. \frac{1}{2}, 8\sqrt{10}) that are graded by symbolic verification rather than string equality.

InsightReplay injection.

InsightReplay is a single post-hoc edit of the baseline response: once the baseline emits the thinking-close marker, we (i) ask the model to enumerate the important conclusions of its own thinking (ii) splice a self-verification block back in before the thinking-close marker; and (iii) let the model continue from that point until it re-emits a thinking-close marker and writes a fresh final answer. The block is phrased in the model’s first person so that, embedded inside the thinking block, it reads as a continuation of the internal monologue rather than an external instruction. Concretely the block contains:

  • •

    an opening line “Wait, before I commit to a final answer, let me restate what’s being asked and double-check the key conclusions I’ve been relying on”;

  • •

    a one-line restatement of the user’s header and the question, so the model does not drift from the task in a long thinking stream;

  • •

    a numbered list of the extracted insights under “Key conclusions so far:

D.4 Datasets and Preprocessing

We use four benchmarks. AIME 2025/2026 concatenates the official problem sets of both years, yielding 6060 short-answer problems (3030 per year) with non-negative integer answers; each record carries a <year>-<idx> identifier and the gold answer string. GPQA Diamond is the full 198198-question Diamond split; the upstream release already embeds the four answer choices into each problem’s question field in their original order (mixing “A. …”, “A) …”, and “a) …” styles across problems), with the structured choices field left null, so we do not shuffle the options and we do not append choice lines on our side – the model sees the question verbatim as released. LiveCodeBench v5 is a fixed 6262-problem uniform subsample of the full 880880-problem v5 release, drawn once to bound the compute cost of running 30B-class models with k=16k=16 samples and ∼20,000{\sim}20{,}000-token CoT lengths; the subsample is shipped with the data files, so all models see the identical 6262-problem subset, with the official hidden test cases attached verbatim. HMMT (Feb & Nov 2025) concatenates the MathArena releases of HMMT February 2025 and HMMT November 2025, yielding 6060 short-answer problems (3030 per contest, sources MathArena/hmmt_feb_2025 and MathArena/hmmt_nov_2025); unlike AIME, HMMT gold answers are arbitrary LaTeX expressions (rationals, radicals, exact closed forms) rather than integers in [0,999][0,999], so we keep them as raw strings and defer simplification to the symbolic grader (Section D.5). We apply no few-shot exemplars, no rephrasing of the math/science text, and no rewriting of the code prompts.

D.5 Evaluation Protocol

The per-sample correct flag is computed by first stripping the model’s thinking block (everything up to and including the last thinking-close marker) and then applying dataset-specific extraction:

  • •

    AIME. The post-think tail is searched for an integer answer using an ordered list of patterns: ⟨\langleAnswer⟩N⟨\rangle\,N\,\langle/Answer⟩\rangle, \boxed{N}, \Answer{N}, “Answer: N” (with markdown bold/italic tolerated around the word “Answer” and between the colon and the digit), and a final “open ⟨\langleAnswer⟩\rangle without a closing tag” fallback. The first pattern that matches wins; ties within a pattern resolve to the last occurrence. Grading is exact integer comparison against the gold answer.

  • •

    GPQA Diamond. The same priority list adapted to single-letter answers A–D. We deliberately do not match “Option A/B/C/D” phrases inside the reasoning, which would otherwise silently override the model’s actual final answer with the last-mentioned option. Grading is case-insensitive letter equality.

  • •

    LiveCodeBench v5. The last ```python ... ``` block in the post-think tail is taken as the candidate solution and executed in a Docker sandbox (python:3.10-slim, --network none, --cpus 1, --memory 2g) against the full hidden test suite. The runner walks all test cases serially within a single sandbox invocation under a 2020-second wall-clock budget covering all tests for that candidate; a sample is correct iff every test passes. We grade 88 candidates in parallel via a process pool. Function-style tests call Solution().<func>(*args); stdin-style tests pipe the input to python solution.py and compare stdout (after stripping leading/trailing whitespace) against the expected output.

  • •

    HMMT. A LaTeX-aware grader is used because gold answers are arbitrary symbolic expressions. We first extract the candidate’s final answer from the post-think tail with a brace-counting scan over the last \boxed{...} (brace counting handles nested {} that a flat regex would mis-balance), with end-of-text fallbacks to $$ ... $$, \[ ... \], inline $ ... $ (with a leading “lhs ==” stripped), and finally a bare standalone final line. All fallbacks are restricted to the end of the response so math fragments mid-reasoning cannot win. Equivalence is checked with the math_verify library (HuggingFace MathArena) configured with float_rounding=3 (∼5×10−4{\sim}5{\times}10^{-4} tolerance) plus two robustness fallbacks: (i) if the candidate contains \pm, we expand it into both signed branches and additionally retry the comma-joined two-solution form, since the prompt asks for multi-solution sets to be packed into a single \boxed{} separated by commas; (ii) if symbolic verification fails, we evaluate gold and candidate to 3030-digit sympy floats and accept on relative tolerance 10−310^{-3}, catching cases where a model truncates a decimal just inside the symbolic-rounding cutoff. This setup judges \sqrt{640} equivalent to 8\sqrt{10} and 0.5 equivalent to \frac{1}{2}, while keeping 0.6 and \frac{1}{2} distinct.

This subsection illustrates the InsightReplay inference pipeline (one extraction + one verification round) on a concrete example from our evaluation runs.

The probability that BB is a nonempty set with the property that the least common multiple of its elements is 20252025 is mn\frac{m}{n}, where mm and nn are relatively prime positive integers. Find m+nm+n.

(AIME 2025, Problem 22; correct answer is 237237. We use gemma-4-e4b-it for this example.)

The verification pass catches and corrects the arithmetic slip from Pass 1, flipping the answer from the incorrect 233233 to the correct 237237. The original reasoning chain was almost entirely sound, and a single concrete checklist of the model’s own intermediate claims was enough to surface and resolve the error without any external feedback.

Appendix E SWE-Bench Evaluation

To evaluate the effectiveness of InsightReplay on real-world software-engineering tasks, we conduct experiments on SWE-Bench-Verified [26], a benchmark consisting of GitHub issues paired with corresponding test cases that verify whether the issue has been resolved.

Dataset.

We randomly select 100100 instances from SWE-Bench-Verified. Each instance contains a natural-language bug report, a Docker image with the target repository checked out at the relevant commit under /testbed, and a set of test cases (both fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass) for evaluation.

Model and Inference Setup.

We use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B as the base model, served via vLLM [30] with 44-way data parallelism across 44 GPUs. The vLLM server is configured with a maximum model length of 262,143262{,}143 tokens, 0.90.9 GPU memory utilization, and the Hermes tool-call parser (--tool-call-parser hermes) to enable native function-calling support. For generation, we set temperature to 1.01.0, top-pp to 0.950.95, and the maximum output tokens to 30,00030{,}000.

Agent Architecture.

The model operates in an agentic loop with access to six tools: file_read, file_edit, file_write, grep, glob, and bash, all scoped to the /testbed directory inside a Docker container. Each tool is registered as a native function schema in the chat-completion API, allowing the model to invoke tools through structured tool-call messages rather than text-based parsing. The agent iterates for up to 5050 turns per sample (max_turns=50). Each turn consists of a model generation followed by tool execution. A prompt-guard mechanism monitors the estimated prompt token count and stops the agent early if it approaches the context-window limit of 40,96040{,}960 tokens (with a 512512-token margin). When the model determines the task is complete, it outputs the token DONE to terminate the loop. The final patch is extracted via git diff from the Docker container.

Sampling and Evaluation.

For each of the 100100 instances, we independently sample k=8k=8 trajectories, yielding 800800 candidate patches in total. Each candidate patch is evaluated by applying it to a fresh Docker container with the original repository state, installing necessary dependencies, and running the instance-specific test suite. A candidate is considered successful if all fail-to-pass tests now pass and all pass-to-pass tests remain passing. We report the candidate-level pass rate, i.e., the fraction of all 800800 candidate patches that resolve the issue.

Compared Methods.

We compare three prompting strategies, all sharing the same agent architecture, tools, and inference hyperparameters:

  • •

    CoT Zero-shot: The system prompt instructs the model to think explicitly and concretely before each action and follow a five-step workflow: (1) understand the bug report, (2) reproduce the bug, (3) inspect relevant source files, (4) analyze the root cause and apply a fix, and (5) re-run tests to confirm resolution. No few-shot examples are provided.

  • •

    CoT Few-shot: Extends the CoT zero-shot prompt with three detailed few-shot examples demonstrating best practices: understanding the issue before patching, preferring narrow inspection and minimal edits, and always validating with the original failure mode.

  • •

    InsightReplay (Ours): Uses the same five-step workflow but introduces a structured <Finding>...</Finding> mechanism. After each high-level workflow step, the model is required to output exactly one <Finding> block summarizing what was learned in that step. Generation stops at the closing tag, and the accumulated insights are rolled up into a summary message that replaces the growing conversation history. This compresses the context while preserving key insights and enforces a disciplined step-by-step progression. The system prompt also includes a detailed few-shot example illustrating the full five-step InsightReplay workflow.

Results.

Table 3 reports candidate-level pass rates. InsightReplay achieves 29.75%29.75\% (238/800238/800), outperforming both CoT Zero-shot (23.12%23.12\%, 185/800185/800) and CoT Few-shot (20.87%20.87\%, 167/800167/800). Relative to the stronger CoT baseline, this is an absolute gain of 6.636.63 percentage points and a relative improvement of approximately 28.7%28.7\%.

Appendix F Length-Sweep Protocol Details

To jointly characterize the relationship between compute budget and accuracy for the length sweep in Section 4.3, we apply the following bin-based visualization protocol per (model, dataset, method) triple.

Per-problem binning.

For each problem, we independently sample k=16k=16 baseline completions (temperature 1.01.0, top-pp 0.950.95), producing 1616 thinking trajectories of varying length. We sort these 1616 samples by completion tokens (ascending) and bin them uniformly into 88 length levels (22 samples per level). Crucially, this binning is done per problem, not globally across all problems: since problems differ substantially in intrinsic difficulty, a global token-based binning would conflate length with difficulty (a “short” bin would be dominated by easy problems, while a “long” bin would be dominated by hard problems). Per-problem binning instead identifies, for each problem, its 88 relative length levels (very-short, short, medium, …\ldots, very-long), so that within each level we compare samples that come from the same set of problems—isolating the length effect from the difficulty effect. Figure 6 illustrates this procedure schematically.

Sample-level pairing for VO/IR.

The corresponding VO\mathrm{VO} / IR1\mathrm{IR1} / IR3\mathrm{IR3} samples strictly inherit the baseline’s token ordering: each VO/IR/IR3 sample is paired to its source baseline sample (sorted by that baseline’s token count). This pairing ensures that within any given length level, all four methods compare samples extended from the same set of baseline starting points, isolating the method’s contribution from sampling variance.

Per-level statistics.

Within each length level, we record two statistics:

  • •

    xx = the mean of the 22 samples’ actual completion tokens (baseline curve = baseline’s own tokens; the other three methods = baseline tokens + injected insights + extended generation tokens);

  • •

    yy = the level’s accuracy (mean of {0,1}\{0,1\} correctness).

Cross-benchmark aggregation.

We first compute the 88 levels’ (x,y)(x,y) values per problem, then average over all problems to obtain the 88 data points for each (model, dataset, method) triple. For the cross-benchmark merged curves shown in Figures 4 and 7, we equally weight the 88 data points across AIME / GPQA / LiveCodeBench / HMMT (each benchmark contributing 1/41/4), to avoid the largest dataset (GPQA, n=3168n=3168) dominating the merged curve.

Results on ∼8\sim 8B-scale models.

Figure 7 reports the length-sweep curves for the three ∼8\sim 8B-scale models (Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-E4B, and R1-Distill-Qwen-7B), applying the same protocol as in Section 4.3. The same two patterns observed at the 3030B scale—rightward shift of the optimal CoT length and upward shift of the peak accuracy—hold here as well, indicating that the inverted-U reshaping predicted by Theorems 1 and 2 is robust across model scales.

Appendix G Post-Training Details

All experiments are implemented on top of the open-source verl RL training framework [31], using its FSDP2 actor backend and vLLM rollout engine.

This appendix lists the full set of hyperparameters used for the InsightReplay RL study reported in the main text. Both the baseline (standard CoT rollout) and the InsightReplay run share identical settings: same base model, same dataset, same optimizer, same KL/clip configuration, same rollout sampler, same length budget, and the same compute topology. The two runs differ in exactly one configuration line — the InsightReplay run additionally sets actor_rollout_ref.rollout.agent.default_agent_loop=
insight_replay_agent, which activates the rollout-time continuation-cue injection described in Section 5; all remaining values below are shared.

Compute and parallelism.
  • •

    Hardware: 1616 nodes ×\times 88 GPUs (NVIDIA H800) =128=128 GPUs total.

  • •

    Training framework: verl with FSDP2; rollout engine: vLLM.

  • •

    Ulysses sequence-parallel size: 22; FSDP shard size: 88; rollout tensor-parallel size: 11 (one vLLM instance per GPU, 128128 instances total).

  • •

Rollout continuation cue.

For the InsightReplay rollout, once the policy emits the end-of-sequence token, we append the following fixed continuation cue before allowing generation to continue under the same response-length budget:

Wait, before I commit to a final answer, let me restate what’s being asked and cross-verify by a completely different method than what I used above. The user’s request: {question} Key conclusions so far:

This cue is inserted with response​_​mask=0\mathrm{response\_mask}{=}0, so the injected tokens affect the model only as conditioning context and never contribute directly to the policy loss.

Training-curve smoothing for visualization.

In Figure 5, for each metric we additionally overlay a smooth trend line obtained by fitting a degree-33 polynomial f^​(t)=∑k=03ak​tk\hat{f}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{3}a_{k}\,t^{k} to the per-step validation values (ti,yi)(t_{i},y_{i}) via ordinary least squares:

(a0,a1,a2,a3)=arg⁡min⁡∑ia⁡(yi−f^​(ti))2.(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},a_{3})\,=\,\arg\min_{a}\;\sum_{i}\bigl(y_{i}-\hat{f}(t_{i})\bigr)^{2}.

We then evaluate f^\hat{f} on 200200 equally spaced points spanning the observed training-step range and render the resulting curve as a dashed line. This fit is used purely as a visual smoother: it suppresses per-evaluation noise so that the relative trend between the two runs is easier to read at a glance. We do not draw any quantitative conclusion from the polynomial coefficients themselves.

Appendix H Alternative Training Method

This appendix documents an earlier attempt to train the multi-round InsightReplay structure directly, rather than inducing it at rollout time with a fixed continuation cue. The pipeline has two stages: we first construct supervised multi-round traces, and then optimize the policy with a training procedure that explicitly mirrors the round-wise visibility pattern used at inference time.

H.1 Method Overview

Base model and goal.

We start from Qwen3.5-9B-Base [21]. The goal of this alternative design is to make the multi-round reasoning structure explicit during training: each round exposes only the question, the currently visible reasoning context, and the replayed intermediate insights that should be accessible at that round.

Stage 1: Supervised multi-round trace construction.

To obtain SFT data in the target format, we sample 2,0002{,}000 math problems from DAPO-Math-17K [29]. For each problem, a strong teacher model, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, generates a full solution, which we then decompose into a sequence of reasoning steps and compact intermediate insights. We convert these into multi-round targets where all non-final rounds contain a reasoning segment together with an intermediate insight, and the last round produces the final answer. This procedure yields 1,8921{,}892 valid problems and 8,1028{,}102 SFT training entries. A concrete example appears in Appendix H.3.

Stage 2: Direct multi-round RL training.

Our RL training procedure consists of two steps, illustrated in Figure 8.

In Step 1, we start from the standard causal mask and add a round-level visibility mask over the concatenated multi-round response. This makes the intended computation explicit: at each round, the model can attend only to the original question, the relevant reasoning tokens, and the replayed insights that should be visible in that round, while all other tokens are masked out on top of the causal constraint. However, this alone creates a RoPE mismatch: masked tokens become invisible under attention, but they still occupy positions during training, so the relative distance between two visible tokens no longer matches the rollout setting in which those masked tokens are physically absent.

In Step 2, we regroup each training case by round. For every round, we delete all masked-out tokens, keep only the tokens visible in that round, and then bundle the resulting per-round traces from the same case for joint optimization. This yields contiguous position_ids that match rollout exactly. For the advantage, standard GRPO uses a sample-wise normalized quantity within a prompt group, e.g.,

AiGRPO=Ri−mean⁡({Rj})std⁡({Rj}).A_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{R_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\{R_{j}\})}{\mathrm{std}(\{R_{j}\})}.

In our alternative design, we instead assign the same case-level reward to every round from the same case and use Ar=R−bA_{r}=R-b for all rounds rr, reusing the same shared advantage across the bundled round-level traces.

This construction is methodologically faithful to the intended multi-round computation, but in practice it is substantially more expensive than the rollout-time cue-injection protocol used in the main paper and did not produce comparable gains on AIME 2025.

H.2 SFT Data Construction Details

Source Data.

We sample 2,0002{,}000 math problems from DAPO-Math-17K [29], a large-scale mathematical reasoning dataset.

Solution Generation.

For each sampled problem, we use Qwen3.5-397B-A17B to generate a complete solution in non-think mode, with temperature τ=0.7\tau=0.7 and top-p=0.95p=0.95.

Post-hoc insight Construction.

Each generated solution is then decomposed into a multi-round insight format as follows:

  1. 1.

    The full solution is split into logical reasoning steps (up to 88 steps).

  2. 2.

    Each reasoning step is summarized into a concise insight (1–2 sentences, up to 256256 tokens) via a separate model call.

  3. 3.

    Multi-turn SFT entries are constructed so that each round contains a reasoning step in <think>...</think> followed by an intermediate conclusion in <finding>...</finding> tags, with the final round producing the answer.

This process yields 1,8921{,}892 valid cases and 8,1028{,}102 SFT training entries. The average number of insight rounds per problem is 3.33.3, with a maximum of 99 rounds.

This subsection illustrates the multi-round insight format with a concrete example from our RL training rollout. The model solves the problem in 33 rounds: two insight rounds followed by one answer round. At each round, the model receives all accumulated context (previous reasoning and insights) and generates the next step.

H.4 SFT Hyperparameters

We fine-tune for one epoch with the following setup:

  • •

    Learning rate: 1×10−51\times 10^{-5}

  • •

    Maximum sequence length: 40,00040{,}000 tokens

  • •

    Global batch size: 128128

    Micro batch size per GPU: 44

  • •

    Hardware: 88 GPUs with FSDP

  • •

    Gradient checkpointing enabled

  • •

    No padding mode with right truncation

H.5 RL Setup

We apply GRPO [28] in two settings: a insight-enabled rollout and a insight-disabled baseline. The RL training set is DAPO-Math-15K, a 15,91715{,}917-problem subset of DAPO-Math-17K. Evaluation is conducted on AIME 2025 [18], with 88 rollouts per problem and mean@1 accuracy as the validation metric.

Reward Function.

We use the DAPO reward manager with the same soft overlong penalty as in the main post-training experiment. The model’s answer is extracted from the last Answer: line, normalized, and compared against the ground truth, yielding a correctness reward of +1.0+1.0 for correct answers and −1.0-1.0 for incorrect ones. In addition, we enable the soft overlong penalty to discourage trajectories that approach the maximum response budget: overlong_buffer.enable=True, the penalty factor is 1.01.0, and max_resp_len passed to the reward matches the rollout max_response_length.

RL Hyperparameters.

Both experiments use the following shared configuration on 88 NVIDIA H200 GPUs:

  • •

    Algorithm: GRPO with token-level loss aggregation

  • •

    Sequence parallelism (Ulysses SP): 88

  • •

    Rollout tensor parallelism: 22

  • •

    Global training batch size: 6464 prompts

  • •

    Rollout nn: 88 responses per prompt (512512 total samples per step)

  • •

    PPO mini-batch size: 3232

  • •

    Learning rate: 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} with 1010 warmup steps

  • •

    KL loss coefficient: 0.0010.001

  • •

    Maximum prompt length: 27,00027{,}000 tokens

  • •

    Maximum response length: 25,00025{,}000 tokens

  • •

    Total training: 55 epoch

  • •

    Validation frequency: every 2020 steps

Insight-Mode Configuration.

In the insight-enabled experiment, rollouts use multi-round generation with up to 55 insight rounds per problem. At each round, the model produces a reasoning step and an intermediate conclusion; all previous reasoning steps and insights remain in context for the next round. The rollout continues until either the maximum number of turns is reached or the model fails to emit a well-formed <finding>...</finding> tag.

Baseline Configuration.

In the insight-disabled experiment, the model generates a single continuous response per problem without any multi-round structure.

H.6 Controlled Variables

To ensure a fair comparison, both experiments:

  • •

    use identical RL hyperparameters;

  • •

    are evaluated on the same AIME 2025 benchmark with the same 88-rollout mean@1 protocol; and

  • •

    differ only in whether the multi-round insight rollout is enabled.

H.7 Experiment Results

Figure 9 summarizes the validation performance of the alternative training method over a unified training budget of 420420 steps. As in the main post-training comparison, we track best​@​32\mathrm{best@32}, maj​@​32\mathrm{maj@32}, and mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32} on AIME 2025 throughout training.

The outcome is mixed. By the end of the 420420-step budget, the InsightReplay variant overtakes the baseline on both mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32} and best​@​32\mathrm{best@32}, indicating a late advantage in average sample quality and upper-tail performance. However, maj​@​32\mathrm{maj@32} remains consistently below the baseline, suggesting that this training recipe does not improve sample-level consistency in the same way.

We also emphasize that these experiments were stopped after exactly 420420 steps rather than trained further. In addition, this direct multi-round training mode is substantially more expensive operationally. Each InsightReplay rollout must merge multiple rounds into a single training example, and the prompt grows longer at later rounds because more reasoning and insight tokens are carried forward. As a result, token cost increases over the course of a single rollout. For this reason, despite the late crossover on mean​@​32\mathrm{mean@32} and best​@​32\mathrm{best@32}, we ultimately did not adopt this training strategy in the main paper.
